live_attach.answer_text: We held one continuous Gospel story - the harmony we read in worship, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete. The four accounts had been woven into a single telling, and for some two hundred years that one story was what 'the Gospel' meant in our churches. Alongside it we read the Law and the Prophets as one long promise pointing toward him. We did not claim living eyewitnesses - a century and more stood between us and the events. Our own cherished story says the apostle Addai came to our king and set the church's life in order, but we will tell you honestly: that is our legend, written down generations later, not a document from the beginning. What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. When the sources begin, the practices are already there - assembly on the first day, the covenant already established, the one woven Gospel already our standard. A church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood, and the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both of those things are true, and our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence.

live_attach.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. With Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we say of God's own character? We knew him as faithful - not because he kept the blow away, but because he stood with the persecuted. Our teacher answered the hardest taunt thrown at us - that our prayers had not stopped the killing - with a roll-call: Abel, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, and Jesus himself, all persecuted. God's faithfulness, we meant, is longer than one generation's rescue. His answer was never exemption; it was presence, and resurrection after.

We knew him also as mystery - not unknown, but too great to be pinned down. Our way of speaking about him ran through symbol, through raza. A symbol is not a stand-in chosen at will; it is bound to the truth - the shrara - it carries, and it carries some of that truth's hidden power. We sang God more than we dissected him. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better praised than taken apart.

And we knew him as the One who gives himself. The Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own title for Christ - left his place with God and made his home among us. That same word, Ihidaya, is also our word for the vowed celibate: the Single One, undivided for God. The two senses share one root - to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

What we argued about among ourselves was exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name. Our picture of God was not settled by being unopposed. It was settled by being defended.

live_attach.answer_text:
Who settled it when our own people disagreed about doctrine? The honest first answer is: it was still being worked out, and the record shows us the working itself, not a finished system.

There were bishops. Nisibis remembered its own line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council held at Nicaea. There were synods: our own teacher - the sage - drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And there were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our own years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

What did we actually do, in practice? Disputed belief was met with teaching - with answers in writing, and with our own boundary. When Bardaisan or Marcion or Mani taught something we judged false, we answered them by name. Our sharpest voice sang against them in madrashe - teaching hymns - and wrote prose refutations. We would not share their communion. That was the boundary held, more than any court verdict handed down.

What evidence tells us it worked that way? The writings themselves. The sage's twenty-three letters - his tahwyata, his Demonstrations - survive with their own dates written into them, year by year, some of them composed while the persecution was still happening. The poet's hymns were copied and kept, and they name the rivals they answer. And one synodical letter, signed in the name of assembled bishops and clergy, survives attributed to the sage - not from his own hand alone, but from a gathered authority he wrote for.

What we cannot show you is a constitution, or a manual saying who outranked whom in every case. Office, vow, and teaching ran side by side to our last year, and which of them finally held was never settled in our own time.

live_attach.answer_text:
Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. One of them said faith is like a building: it sits on one foundation stone and goes up slowly, piece by piece - prayer, fasting, love, each added over time. A building is not finished in a day, and neither is a believer.

What they warned against was something different: taking God apart like a puzzle to be solved. Even our own poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn - each a madrasha, our teaching-song. And a debater once threw the hardest one at our teacher: if your faith were real, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? He did not dodge it, and he did not pretend it was easy.

The one who could not quiet their own head, who could not pray, who felt themselves failing - for that person we had what we called the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

So no, doubt was not treated as sin among us. What was deadly was the shame that kept someone from naming it.

live_attach.answer_text: No - not in the way that question usually means. We said that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone, even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding - a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. The sage put it this way: of all who are born, who have taken on a body, there is only one who carried no wound. Everyone else enters already wounded - that much we held. But a wound is not the same thing as a verdict of guilty. A wound needs healing, and that is why we called our Lord the Physician. He came for the wounded, not to condemn them for being wounded. Our teachers talked like field surgeons, not like judges. And we preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross. The distinction matters: we did not say infants are born condemned. We said they are born into a world where death rules, and they need the Physician's healing.

live_attach.answer_text:
We read Scripture for the hidden truth a thing carries, not only the plain thing itself. A word, a story, an image - each is a raza, a symbol bound to the shrara, the truth it discloses. The raza is not a figure we choose at will - it is wed to the truth it shows, and it carries some of that truth's hidden power. So our poet could pick up a pearl and see mysteries woven through it: the kingdom, baptism, the hidden truth inside the ordinary thing. Eden is read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. Type answers type, and the whole of Scripture becomes one long conversation between promise and fulfillment.

The Gospel we read was one continuous story, not four separate books. For all of our years, 'the Gospel' meant the harmony - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed - Tatian's woven account that our congregations heard in worship. Our own sage quoted it, and our poet commented on it, as the Gospel they simply had. So our experience of the Lord's life was narrative wholeness, not four-witness plurality.

And we read knowing the practices we kept went back to the apostles - not because we filed evidence for it the way a court would, but because we told the story. When the sources begin, the practices are already there: the assembly on the first day, the fast, the covenant already established enough to need correcting, the one Gospel already the standard. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The way we claimed it was to tell it - the story of Addai sent to our king, healing him, setting the church's life in order. That is our cherished legend, and we will not pretend otherwise. But practice older than proof is still what we had.

Our native register for all of this was the sung hymn and the typological reading. Argument itself moved by setting type against type, not by building syllogisms. We sang the faith more than we defined it.

live_attach.answer_text:
A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. 

Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. The harmony - the Diatessaron, the one woven Gospel we read in worship - is attested early enough that both our anchor voices simply presuppose it. The sage quotes it, and the poet comments on it. That stands. The covenant order - our vowed sons and daughters, the qyama - stands at our community's core early enough that its first datable witness addresses it as already established and needing correction. The pearl hymn is genuine. The symbolic method - reading by raza and shrara, type answering type - is everywhere in the texts and stands as our native theological register.

But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either. 

Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers. Our argument with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page with no answering voice preserved.

The authority question stays open because the record left it open. Whether the sage was a bishop, and how settled the Persian hierarchy actually was, are unresolved. We will not pretend otherwise.

What survives scrutiny is this: the texts, their dates, the practices they attest, and the honest gaps where the record runs out.

live_attach.answer_text:
They are missing the raza - the symbol - and so they see only the surface. A raza is not decoration, and it is not a figure of speech chosen at will. It is a thing in Scripture or in nature that is bound to the truth - the shrara - it carries, and it even holds some of that truth's hidden power. Our own poet once picked up a pearl, and in it he saw mysteries - not because he invented them, but because the pearl itself carries them. Eden answers to the cross, Adam to Christ, the Jordan to the font. Type answers type, and the whole of Scripture is woven that way - every name, every place, every number a sign pointing toward the one story underneath it all.

When someone reads Genesis and asks only whether it happened the way modern science would measure it, they have walked past the door without seeing it was open. We read for something else: not less than what the words plainly say, but far more than that. A whole chapter's worth of meaning was found in a single pearl. That is not because we were careless with the text - we sang it, quoted it, wove it into every argument we made. It is because we held that Scripture's own words were each a raza, and the shrara they carry is Christ himself, met everywhere the eye is trained to see him.

The other thing they are missing is this: Scripture never arrived alone. It was always carried - by the church's worship, by the one Gospel harmony that gave the story its shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's practice. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals. The question assumes a separation we had not made.

uncited_claim_sentences: When someone reads Genesis and asks only whether it happened the way modern science would measure it, they have walked past the door without seeing it was open.
uncited_before_attach: When someone reads Genesis and asks only whether it happened the way modern science would measure it, they have walked past the door without seeing it was open.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture was supreme and everywhere among us - sung, quoted, woven into every argument we made. But it never arrived alone. It always came carried. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals, because we had not made that separation.

How did Scripture come to us? Through the church's worship first of all. Through the harmony that gave the Gospel its one shape. Through teachers whose word held over time. And through the covenant's own practice - the qyama, the vowed life that stood at our center. We did not read Scripture the way moderns argue about Genesis, as though it were competing with natural knowledge. We read for something else entirely.

Every word was a raza - a symbol bound to the truth it carries, the shrara. Eden pointed to the cross, Adam to Christ, the ark to the church. One of our own picked up a single pearl and saw mysteries enough to fill a hymn. That was how we read: not taking the text apart to test it, but looking through it to the truth it showed.

So if you ask whether Scripture stood alone as our authority, the question itself feels strange to us. It stood first, always. But asking us to pull it away from the singing, the teachers, the covenant's witness, and the community's life - that would be like asking whether a foundation stands alone when the house built on it is what makes the foundation mean anything at all.

sources.spoken_rendering: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side. I discovered that the Son cannot be fully grasped, since he is wholly Light.
sources.speaker: Ephrem the Syrian, The Pearl, Hymn I

live_attach.answer_text:
Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had its bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. The good shepherd gives himself for the flock - that was what we asked of them.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women - the bnay and bnat qyama, the sons and daughters of the covenant - carried a standing of their own. They promised a celibate life for good, stayed in town among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. We also called them ihidaye - the Single Ones - a name that bound their undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten, the Ihidaya himself. That order stood at our community's core early enough that when it first appears in writing, it is already established and needing correction, not founding.

And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name. That standing came from being found trustworthy over time, not from being given an office first.

How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. It took a royal synod, after our own years, to give the Persian church one settled head. Until then, office and vow and teaching ran side by side, and we left that question open.

live_attach.answer_text: No. That is another city's story, not ours. In Edessa, a church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood of 201, and the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces. On the frontier, believers gathered openly on the first day of the week. The catacombs you are thinking of - those belong to Rome's own memory, not to ours.

live_attach.answer_text:
We had medicine for the one who fell. Our own teacher said it this way: for every disease there is medicine, and healing awaits the one who confesses the wound. The believer who broke faith, who sinned and could not carry it anymore, was told to bring it to someone who could help - a shepherd, a teacher, someone trusted. That helper was bound not to shame the wounded person, and not to spread what had been shown in confidence. The fallen one, healed, went back into the congregation's life. That was the craft we had for the believer who stumbled and came back.

But your question goes deeper than that, and we owe you the whole answer. For the one the community itself failed - drove out, refused, or wounded by our own hardness - we have no record of repair at all. Our texts were written by vowed celibates, teachers, bishops. The daughters of the covenant sang in every church, their voices carried our faith to everyone who heard it, and not one line any of them wrote was kept. The enslaved among us left no voice at all - we know the empire held slaves; of their days inside our own churches we cannot tell you one true thing. And our argument with the Jews was real, local, and bitter, kept entirely one-sided - page after page of our own words, with no answering voice preserved and no one among us on record as troubled by that.

So here is what we can honestly say: we had a way back for the believer who sinned and repented. We do not have a record of repair for the ones we ourselves wounded, or drove out, or never heard. That gap is real. We will not fill it with a story we do not have.

live_attach.answer_text:
The Church of the East carries the oldest line that runs from us - what some later centuries called the Nestorian church, and what its own people have always called the Assyrian Church of the East. That communion still worships in Syriac, still reads the Peshitta Scriptures we knew, and still traces itself back through the Persian side of our own world. The Catholicos-Patriarch who leads it today sits in the same succession the Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon organized in 410, the year our own window closes. And the Chaldean Catholic Church, which entered communion with Rome in the sixteenth century but kept the East Syriac liturgy, shares that same root.

But we owe you the honest distance too. The four Gospels as four separate books replaced the one woven Gospel we actually read. The covenant order - our own qyama, the vowed men and women who stayed in town rather than leave for the desert - did not survive as we knew it. Monasticism, which came in from Egypt after our years, took a different shape. And doctrine was settled by councils we never saw, in registers we would recognize but also past.

So the truthful answer is this: the Church of the East is our closest living heir, genuinely descended from the Persian church we knew. But sixteen centuries stand between us and them, and no tradition crosses that span unchanged. We will not claim an identity we cannot show you.

uncited_claim_sentences: The Church of the East carries the oldest line that runs from us - what some later centuries called the Nestorian church, and what its own people have always called the Assyrian Church of the East.
And the Chaldean Catholic Church, which entered communion with Rome in the sixteenth century but kept the East Syriac liturgy, shares that same root.
But we owe you the honest distance too.
Monasticism, which came in from Egypt after our years, took a different shape.
So the truthful answer is this: the Church of the East is our closest living heir, genuinely descended from the Persian church we knew.
But sixteen centuries stand between us and them, and no tradition crosses that span unchanged.

live_attach.answer_text:
We will tell you what we honestly can - the pieces we kept, in the order we can show them - and name plainly where the record runs thin.

Someone came because the word was preached, or because they heard the singing, or because someone they knew already belonged. That first motion - how they first heard, who brought them, what they thought before they believed - our record almost never keeps, because the voices that survive are teachers writing to people already inside, not beginners telling their own stories.

Once they came, they were taught. They heard the Gospel as one continuous story - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the harmony we read in worship. They were taught to read Scripture the way we read it: each thing in it a raza, a symbol bound to the truth it carries. The sage wrote that before baptism, preachers warned the one coming plainly what they were taking on - that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone, and that the new birth they were about to receive was medicine for that wound. How long that teaching lasted, and whether it followed any one set order, our own record does not say.

Then came baptism itself. We sang of the font as a womb, and the one baptized came up from the water clothed in new garments and sealed - marked with the sign. In baptism's second birth, we held, the believer receives the Holy Spirit. That much is solid. What we cannot walk you through is the actual sequence of an assembly on that morning: who stood where, what words were said in what order, what came first and what came next. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying it all out step by step. We kept the hymns and the teaching about what baptism meant. The sequence that held them together on an actual day, our own record never wrote down.

After baptism, the new believer joined the assembly. They gathered with everyone else on the first day of the week. They heard the Gospel sung and read. They fasted when the community fasted. And some - not all, but some - heard a further call: to the qyama, the covenant. The sons and daughters of the covenant vowed a celibate life for good, but they did not leave town. They stayed among their own kin and served: the vigil, the fast, the singing, visiting the sick. They were called ihidaye - the Single Ones - and that name bound them to Christ the Only-Begotten, who is himself the Ihidaya. That vow was already established by the time our earliest datable witness addresses it; it was being corrected, not founded.

What we cannot show you plainly is how formally the covenant order was organized inside our own years - whether it had a written rule, an enclosure, an internal hierarchy. And here is the honest thinness we will not hide: the daughters of the covenant sang in every church, their voices carrying our faith, but not one line written by one of them was kept. We can tell you they were there. We cannot give you their own words.

That is what we can show you of how someone joined us: taught, baptized, gathered - and for some, called further into the covenant. The rest we will not invent.

uncited_claim_sentences: Someone came because the word was preached, or because they heard the singing, or because someone they knew already belonged.
Once they came, they were taught.
Then came baptism itself.
That much is solid.
After baptism, the new believer joined the assembly.
They gathered with everyone else on the first day of the week.
They fasted when the community fasted.

added: How long that teaching lasted, and whether it followed any one set order, our own record does not say.
In baptism's second birth, we held, the believer receives the Holy Spirit.
They heard the Gospel sung and read.
